**Finding submitted: deviation (T4C — Termination for convenience).**

**What the document says:** Section 11.1 locks in a five-year initial term with automatic one-year renewals, and the only exit is non-renewal at the end of the initial or a renewal term (30 days' notice). Section 11.2 limits mid-term termination to uncured material breach or insolvency. There is no convenience right for Corio anywhere in the agreement (the other refund/termination rights found — §3 acceptance failure, §7 warranty, §8 indemnity — are all for-cause).

**Why it fails:** Under the rule's detection guidance, the absence of any customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months is a deviation, and it also falls short of the fallback (60–90 days' notice). Note the direction check: Commerce One has no mid-term convenience right either, which benefits us, so that half of the rule is already satisfied and was left untouched.

**Redline (validated ok:true):** new Section 11.3 inserted after 11.2 granting Corio convenience termination on 30 days' notice, with pro-rata refund of prepaid recurring fees, no early-termination fee or fee acceleration, and confirmation that Commerce One has no convenience right during the term. Existing 11.3 (Effect of Termination) renumbers — that clause's survival protections for Corio's existing customers were deliberately preserved. Refund scope was drafted as prepaid *recurring* fees (maintenance, support, access) rather than all fees, since the license fee is a one-time payment due on acceptance.
